extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy/logic (analytic epistemology and philosophy of language)
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing the epistemology and logic of propositions that contain definite descriptions by distinguishing knowledge-by-acquaintance from knowledge-by-description and prescribing how descriptions must be analysed in propositional content. Focuses on what counts as constituents of judgments/propositions and how meaning and denotation should be treated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of acquaintance
rubrics_metrics.description: I am acquainted with an object when I have a direct cognitive relation to that object, i.e. when I am directly aware of the object itself; acquaintance is the converse of presentation and emphasises the subject-object relational character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acquaintance is not the sort of relation that constitutes judgment but the relation that constitutes presentation; it may persist when the object is not presently before the mind (memory). Use 'acquaintance' to preserve dualism of subject and object and avoid treating the object as part of the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquaintance applies to sense-data and complexes
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary examples of acquaintance are sense-data (e.g. colours, noises) and often complex sense-data (especially visual complexes containing spatially related parts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that direct sensible objects can be complex and may contain constituents; introspective awareness often presents complexes (e.g. 'I am aware of my desire for food' as a complex involving the subject).

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of universals (conceiving)
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to particulars, we can be directly aware of universals (called conceiving), e.g. the universal 'yellow', and universal relations like 'before' or 'resemblance'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To understand general propositional forms (e.g. 'if A before B and B before C then A before C') we must suppose acquaintance with the universal relation itself, not merely instances; this supports analysing propositions involving relations in terms of constituents with which we are acquainted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two basic object-kinds for acquaintance: particulars and universals
rubrics_metrics.description: Objects with which we are acquainted are of two sorts: particulars (existents and complexes involving existents) and universals (objects of which no particular is a constituent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This dichotomy (abstract-concrete) covers all objects of awareness; remember remembered or imagined particulars are still particulars, and universals can be identified with concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: ambiguous vs definite descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: A phrase of the form 'a so-and-so' is an 'ambiguous' description; a phrase of the form 'the so-and-so' (singular) is a 'definite' description. The paper focuses on definite descriptions ('the so-and-so').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing propositions, treat 'the so-and-so' as expressing existence-and-uniqueness conditions to be examined, rather than leaving it unanalyzed as a single constituent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known by description
rubrics_metrics.description: An object is 'known by description' when we know that it is 'the so-and-so' (i.e. that there is one and only one object with that property) and generally we are not acquainted with that object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the man with the iron mask' or 'the candidate who gets most votes' — we can know many propositions about such objects without being acquainted with them personally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merely descriptive knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: We have 'merely descriptive knowledge' of a so-and-so when, though we know there is an object satisfying the description, and perhaps are even acquainted with the actual object, we do not know any proposition of the form 'a is the so-and-so' where 'a' is something with which we are acquainted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish knowing existence/uniqueness from knowing identity to a particular you are acquainted with; mere description limits what further judgments you can meaningfully make about the object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental epistemological principle about propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Every proposition which we can understand must be composed wholly of constituents with which we are acquainted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize this by analysing any proper-name or definite-description occurrence into constituents (sense-data, concepts, existence/uniqueness claims) so that the mind is acquainted with all terms of the supposed relation of judging or supposing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgments and supposing are many-term relations with constituents
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgment (or the relation of supposing) is a many-term relation between the mind and the entities that compose what is judged; the constituents of the judgment are exactly the constituents of the complex which is the judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing whether a subject understands a proposition, check that every term of the proposition corresponds to an object or concept with which the subject is (or could be) acquainted; e.g., in 'A loves B' the distinctive constituents are A, love, and B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper names ordinarily stand for descriptions (only 'I' and 'this' strict names)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common words, even proper names, are usually really descriptions (the content of the thought can generally be expressed by a description). In Russell's sense only 'I' and 'this' are strict proper names of particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume a proper name inserts the denotation as a constituent of a proposition; substitute an appropriate description when analysing propositional content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denotation is not a constituent of propositions; meaning matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The denotation (the actual object) does not occur as a constituent of a proposition in which a descriptive phrase appears; the meaning of the descriptive phrase is relevant to the proposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the author of Waverley is a novelist' can be understood without knowing that the denotation is Scott; different descriptive phrases with same denotation may yield different inferential content, so analyse meanings, not merely denotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyse definite descriptions away (existence & uniqueness plus predication)
rubrics_metrics.description: A phrase like 'the man whose name was Julius Cæsar' must not be treated as a single constituent; instead analyse the phrase so the proposition asserts (i) one-and-only-one existence of the described and (ii) that that one instantiates the predicate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite propositions with definite descriptions into logical form: e.g. 'the man whose name was Julius Cæsar was assassinated' -> 'one and only one man was called Julius Cæsar, and that man was assassinated.' This prevents treating the description as a constituent and preserves acquaintance-with-constituents principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject idea-intermediary (no 'ideas' between mind and object)
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory that judgments are composed of 'ideas' (mental entities standing between mind and object) is mistaken; acquaintance is a direct relation and does not presuppose internal 'ideas'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid analyses that posit internal mental 'ideas' as constituents of judgments; such views lead to regress (idea of idea of object) and obscure the direct relation of acquaintance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reformulation of law of contradiction to avoid Meinongian problems
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of contradiction should be stated as 'no proposition is both true and false' rather than 'A is not both B and not B', which only applies to subject-predicate style propositions; this avoids treating propositions about non-existent denotations as exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a proposition-centered formulation of logical laws to ensure propositions about non-existent or self-contradictory descriptions (e.g. 'the round square') are properly handled as propositions that can be true or false but not both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning-denotation regress caution
rubrics_metrics.description: If one treats the denotation of a descriptive phrase as the denotation of its meaning, explaining propositions in terms of identity of denotation leads to an infinite regress of meanings and denotations (M, M', ...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid taking denotation-as-constituent as primitive; instead provide an analysis that breaks descriptive phrases into variables/conditions (existence/uniqueness and predicates) to stop the regress.
